Constructing a Funnel: An Identity, Not a Model

A funnel decomposes one number into ordered ones. Everything an expert argues about lies in what the decomposition does not license you to conclude.

1. Two Desks, Three Weeks Apart

On 2 September 2025, Sunaina Kothari, director of product at Praanali Credit, a personal-loan app licensed to a Bengaluru NBFC, was handed a one-line brief by her chief executive: explain why August cost ₹9.03 crore in acquisition spend and produced 4,556 fewer loans than July. Installs had risen from 410,000 to 430,000. Disbursals had fallen from 29,768 to 25,212. Cost per funded loan had gone from ₹2,892 to ₹3,582 against a board-committed ceiling of ₹3,000 and a contribution margin of about ₹4,100 per loan. The board met on 26 September.

Praanali's head of growth had already reached a verdict. The seven-step funnel showed e-mandate registration — the eNACH auto-debit setup that must succeed before money moves — converting at 71.0% in August against 78.0% in July. That was the largest absolute fall of any step. Fix the mandate screen, he argued, and August repairs itself. Sunaina's instinct was that he had read the table correctly and drawn the wrong conclusion, but she could not yet say why in a sentence a board would accept.

Three weeks later and 980 kilometres west, Yusuf Rangwala, vice-president of product at Surangam, an AI claims-adjudication copilot sold to general insurers, faced a different species of the same problem. Surangam's largest customer, a private general insurer, had a ₹4.2 crore annual contract with a renewal clause tied to an "AI-assisted closure rate" of at least 55%. Surangam's dashboard reported 60.9%. The insurer's own analytics team reported 26.0%. Neither number was wrong. Both were funnels built from the same events with different entry criteria, and ₹4.2 crore turned on which denominator the contract had meant.

These two scenes frame the argument of this page. The funnel is among the most reliable instruments in product analytics precisely because, at its core, it is an accounting identity: overall conversion is the product of the step-to-step rates, always, with no assumptions. Every serious dispute practitioners have about funnels — Sunaina's and Yusuf's included — arises the moment someone uses the identity to make a claim it cannot support: a claim about cause, about what a fix will yield, about whose population is being counted, or about what the number will still mean after the organisation starts managing it.

2. The Idea, and the Four Schools That Read It Differently

Define terms precisely. A funnel is an ordered set of named events s1…sn, an entry criterion that defines which subjects enter at s1, a maturity window w within which a subject must reach later steps to be counted, an ordering rule (strict sequence or any-order), and a unit of counting (distinct subjects, not events). Step-to-step conversion pi is the share of subjects at si−1 who also reach si inside w. Overall conversion C = ∏ pi. Note what is definitional and what is empirical: the product rule is definitional and cannot fail. The values of pi are empirical. Everything interesting is in the gap.

The lineage is older than software. Elias St. Elmo Lewis's 1898 attention–interest–desire–action sequence gave advertisers a vocabulary for losses they could not observe; the funnel as measurement, rather than metaphor, arrived only when event logging made each stage countable per person. The problem it was invented to solve is narrow and worth stating exactly: a single conversion rate is unactionable because it is an average over a process, and averages over processes hide where the process fails. That is all the funnel promises. Four schools now disagree about how much more it delivers.

The decomposition school, descended from web analytics practice, treats the funnel as the first and cheapest instrument in any investigation. It will sign the proposition that the largest proportional step loss is the correct place to look first. It will not sign the proposition that the largest drop is the correct place to invest — a distinction we make numerically below.

The journey school, whose modern statement is the consumer decision journey literature of the late 2000s and whose analytic tools are path and Sankey analysis, holds that real behaviour loops, re-enters and arrives by unmodelled routes, so any linear funnel is a lossy projection of a graph. It will sign that a funnel systematically undercounts conversions that took an unmodelled path. It will not sign the caricature attributed to it — that measurement should be abandoned. It measures state transitions instead, and pays for that richness in interpretability.

The survival school imports discrete-time hazard modelling from reliability engineering and biostatistics. Its central claim is that reaching a step is a time-to-event outcome with right-censoring, so a conversion rate computed without a maturity window is a biased estimator, not merely an imprecise one. It will sign that every funnel needs a stated window justified by the observed completion-time distribution. It will not sign that a scalar rate is ever a sufficient summary.

The causal school insists the funnel is purely descriptive. Because fixing an upstream step changes the composition of everyone downstream, any uplift projected from a funnel is an upper bound, and only a randomised experiment licenses a claim about what an intervention will yield. It will sign that funnels are excellent for hypothesis generation and poor for forecasting. It will not sign making step rates the primary goal metric of a team, because a step rate is trivially improvable by changing who enters it.

An expert holds all four simultaneously and knows which is binding in a given room. Sunaina's dispute was a decomposition-versus-causal dispute. Yusuf's was a definitional dispute that no school resolves, because the answer is contractual rather than analytical.

3. Mechanics: The Decomposition, Worked

Sunaina's first act was to publish the funnel with its definitions in the header, because a step rate without an entry criterion, a window and an ordering rule is not a number anyone can argue with. Entry: distinct devices with a first app-open in the calendar month. Window: 30 days from entry. Order: strict. Unit: distinct applicant identity after device-to-PAN resolution.

The second act is the one that separates practitioners. A conversion rate is a product, so changes in it are additive in logarithms: ln C = ∑ ln pi, therefore Δln C = ∑ Δln pi. This gives an exact, non-overlapping attribution of a conversion change across steps — something percentage-point differences cannot do, because a 3-point fall at a step with 78% base is not comparable to a 3-point fall at a step with 48% base. July's rates were 46.0 / 68.0 / 50.0 / 62.0 / 78.0 / 96.0, giving C = 7.26%. August's gave 5.86%. The ratio is 0.808, a log change of −0.2137.

So the head of growth had the arithmetic right. The step he named contributed 44% of the loss. Sunaina's objection was about the next inference, and it turns on two quantities the table does not contain: downstream survival and reachable headroom. The value of repairing step i is entrants × (∏j≠i pj) × Δpi — that is, the gain is proportional to the product of every other step's rate, so a late step converts its own gains almost entirely into outcomes while an early step's gains are taxed by everything after it. But Δpi is not the observed gap. It is the part of the gap an intervention can actually close.

Three findings inverted the ranking. First, roughly four of the seven lost mandate points came from authentication failures at two public-sector banks whose netbanking mandate flow Praanali does not control; the reachable portion was three points, worth about 1,065 loans, after six weeks of work. Second, the three-point KYC fall dated precisely to 8 August, when a new video-KYC vendor went live with a stricter liveness threshold — self-inflicted, fully reversible, one week of work, 1,164 loans. Third, the KYC-to-offer step is not a drop at all. It is an eligibility gate: underwriting declined those applicants on bureau data. Its decline reflected a deliberate risk-policy tightening after a rise in early delinquency. Treating it as leakage would have meant asking a product team to "improve" a number the risk committee had lowered on purpose.

4. Conditions, Stated as Claims You Can Test

The funnel is the right instrument when four claims hold, and each is checkable rather than a matter of taste.

Claim one: the population is monotonically nested. Every subject at step i passed through step i−1. Test it by counting subjects who reached si without ever firing si−1; if that share exceeds a few per cent, the order is wrong or a path is unmodelled. Praanali passes: regulation forces the sequence. Surangam fails: adjudicators open suggestions for documents whose extraction fell below the confidence threshold, and documents are re-uploaded after manual correction, so a single claim can occupy two positions in the same day's funnel.

Claim two: the steps are within one attempt at one goal. A funnel measures progress inside an attempt; a retention curve measures returns across calendar time. Praanali passes. Surangam's commercial funnel — pilot signed, first integration, hundredth claim, expansion — spans nine months and multiple humans, and behaves more like a pipeline of negotiated states than a behavioural funnel.

Claim three: the window exceeds the completion-time distribution of the slowest step. Praanali's application-to-disbursal median is 2.4 days and its 95th percentile 14 days, so a 30-day window is defensible and a 7-day window is not. Test it by plotting cumulative conversion against days since entry and reading where the curve flattens.

Claim four: the composition of entrants is stable, or is being controlled for. If the mix of who enters changes, step rates move without anything about the product changing. Praanali fails this badly in August, as the next section shows. Surangam's document mix is set by the insurer's channel mix and is not stable either.

The funnel becomes actively misleading in three situations. When steps are gates rather than behaviours, it invites product work against a policy decision. When entry is uncontrolled and marketing can change the mix at will, step rates become a measure of traffic quality masquerading as a measure of product quality. And when the interesting question is whether the path should exist at all, the funnel's framing quietly rules that question out: it can tell you that 54% of Praanali's applicants abandon before KYC completes, but it cannot suggest a pre-approved offer flow in which most of those users never do KYC at all.

5. Hard Edge Cases and the Organisational Seams

Two-sided. Naharmandi, a construction-materials marketplace, runs a buyer funnel — RFQ posted, at least one quote within four hours, quote viewed, order placed — whose second step converts at 67% in Pune and 34% in Nagpur with an identical buyer interface. The step is not a property of the buyer funnel at all; it is supplier liquidity wearing a buyer-funnel costume. Naharmandi's regression of quote rate on active suppliers per category found that a 10% increase in live suppliers raised RFQ-to-quote by 4.6 points. The correct response to the worst step in the buyer funnel was a supplier-recruitment programme in Nagpur. Mature marketplaces handle this by refusing to publish a single-sided funnel without the other side's liquidity metric on the same page; less mature ones ship three buyer-side redesigns first.

Hardware plus software. Doabgrid Instruments sells solar-pump controllers to agri-cooperatives. Of 1,000 units shipped in a quarter, technician job sheets recorded 906 installed, telemetry recorded 812 first heartbeats, 604 owners paired the mobile app and 447 set a first irrigation schedule. The 94-unit gap between installation and heartbeat was not a software funnel drop: 63 of those units sat in a dealer's godown miscounted as installed, and the rest were in blocks with no cellular coverage. A telemetry-only funnel silently attributes distribution and connectivity failures to the product. The expert practice is to reconcile the first instrumented step against a non-telemetry source of truth — dispatch records, job sheets, warranty registrations — and to treat the unobservable physical steps as a named dark segment rather than as noise.

AI-native. Surangam's per-document funnel has a step whose conversion rate is a model property that drifts with the input distribution: the share of documents whose extraction clears the confidence threshold was 77.4% in September and 83% in June, entirely because the insurer's channel mix shifted toward scanned paper forms. Retries make the population non-nested. And the threshold itself is a product lever: lowering it raises step three and lowers step five, moving the drop rather than removing it.

Regulated. Praanali's funnel contains at least three steps whose rates are set by someone other than product — bureau-based underwriting, RBI-mandated cooling-off disclosures, bank-side mandate authentication. Mature lenders split the funnel visibly into a demand funnel (which product owns) and a supply funnel (which risk owns), and report a "product-controllable conversion" alongside the headline figure.

The seams. The most consequential edge case is organisational. When each step has an owner, the funnel becomes a scorecard, and a step rate is trivially improvable by tightening who is allowed to enter it. Praanali's mandate team could raise its own step from 71% to 79% overnight by pre-screening out public-sector-bank customers before the mandate screen — the total would be unchanged and the arbitrage invisible in their dashboard. Mature companies say they prevent this with governance; what they actually do is assign accountability to the product of a contiguous span of steps rather than to any single rate, and require any change to an entry criterion to be published with a before-and-after on the total.

6. Ten Distinctions an Expert Makes

The identity is not a model. The product rule holds by construction, which is why it feels authoritative; but every forecast built on it assumes step rates are independent of one another, and they are not. The tell is a deck projecting overall conversion by multiplying four independently-targeted step improvements. The obvious reading — that the steps are separate systems — is wrong because they share a population.

The biggest drop is rarely the biggest opportunity. Leverage is downstream survival times reachable headroom, not observed gap. The tell is a practitioner who ranks work by step-to-step percentage without asking what fraction of the gap any intervention can close, and who consequently proposes six weeks on a bank-side failure over one week on a self-inflicted vendor threshold.

Gates are not drops. A decline is a decision by the firm; an abandon is a decision by the user. Mixing them produces a funnel in which "improving conversion" means approving riskier borrowers. The tell is a step whose rate moves in perfect step-changes on policy dates rather than drifting. The obvious reading — everything that narrows the population belongs in the funnel — is wrong because funnels exist to direct product work, and product cannot act on credit policy.

Fixing an upstream step degrades the downstream rates. The users a top-of-funnel improvement admits are, by construction, the ones who previously would not enter — the marginal, lower-intent population. They convert worse downstream, so the blended rates of every later step fall. The tell is three downstream steps "regressing" in the month after an upstream win that nobody downstream caused. Section 8 works this through.

Mix shift can move an aggregate step rate the opposite way from every segment in it. The tell is a step whose aggregate rate falls while each segment's rate rises. The obvious reading — the step got worse — is wrong; the composition of who reached it changed. Always decompose a step change into a within-segment component and a mix component before diagnosing anything.

Right-censoring makes recent cohorts look worse than they are. Subjects still in flight are counted in the denominator and not the numerator. Praanali's 4 September cohort read 5.1% when measured on 11 September and matured to 5.9% by day 30 — a 13.6% apparent shortfall that is purely an artefact of measurement date. The tell is a funnel whose recent weeks always slope downward and always revise upward.

Monotonicity is an assumption, not a fact. Retries, back-navigation and re-entry mean a subject can occupy two steps at once. There are two defensible conventions — first-attempt (a subject's outcome is fixed by their first pass) and max-progress (a subject is recorded at the furthest step ever reached) — and they can differ by six percentage points on the same data, as they do at Surangam. The tell is a funnel with no stated retry convention; the right question is not which is correct but which matches the decision being made.

The denominator is a contractual object, not an analytical one. Whose population the rate is a fraction of is a negotiation with whoever will act on it. Yusuf's 60.9% and the insurer's 26.0% are both correct; the dispute is about whether Surangam is accountable for the insurer's postal and branch intake channels. The tell is two organisations quoting different numbers from the same event stream and each assuming the other is mistaken.

An instrumentation change and a behaviour change look identical. An SDK upgrade that drops an event on one Android build produces a clean, plausible, entirely fictitious step decline. The tell is a step-level drop that is discontinuous on a release date and confined to one platform or app version. The obvious reading — users changed — is wrong far more often than teams expect, and the check costs ten minutes.

The funnel you can build today was determined by the taxonomy you designed eighteen months ago. Every funnel question you cannot answer is a past event-design decision. Experts therefore instrument for funnels not yet needed: a step that exists in the interface but fires no event is invisible forever, retroactively. The tell is an analyst who answers "we can't see that" more than once a quarter about steps users clearly take.

7. How It Differs by Product Type and Stage

In consumer products the funnel resolves inside a session or a day, the unit is one person, and the main threats are mix shift and instrumentation. In B2B and enterprise the funnel spans weeks, several of its steps are CRM state changes entered by a human rather than logged events, and the entity that converts is an account, not a user — so the per-user tracking that makes consumer funnels easy is simply unavailable, and step rates are as much a measure of sales process as of product. In platforms and marketplaces the decisive fact is cross-side endogeneity, as Naharmandi shows: a step rate on one side is partly a liquidity measurement of the other. In hardware, the first instrumented step is never the first real step, and reconciliation against physical records is the whole discipline. In AI products, at least one step is a model whose rate drifts with input distribution and can be traded against a later step by moving a threshold.

The stage difference is smaller than commonly claimed, and it is worth saying plainly where it is not real. The mechanics do not change with scale: entry criterion, window, order rule, unit of counting, and the log decomposition are identical at 500 users and 5 million. What changes is the binding constraint. At seed stage, with a few hundred entrants a month, step rates have confidence intervals wide enough that a 6-point move is noise, so the funnel's value is qualitative — it tells a founder which screen to go watch ten people use. At Praanali's scale the funnel's value is the opposite: aggregates are precise enough that the risk is no longer noise but concealment, and the work is segmentation, governance and reconciliation. The genuine stage discontinuity is not analytical but organisational, and it arrives the day steps acquire owners.

8. Three Worked Cases

Case A — Praanali: the mix shift under the mandate step

Before committing six weeks to the mandate screen, Sunaina split the step by the customer's bank. The result reversed the diagnosis.

A shift-share decomposition holds one factor at a time. Holding the July mix and applying the August rates gives 0.65×87.0 + 0.35×64.0 = 78.95%, a within-segment effect of +1.0 point. Holding the July rates and applying the August mix gives 0.30×86.0 + 0.70×63.0 = 69.9%, a mix effect of −8.1 points. The two combine to the observed −7.0. The mandate flow did not get worse. An August performance-marketing push into tier-2 districts had more than doubled the share of customers banking with public-sector banks, whose mandate route had always converted 23 points lower. The product decision was therefore not a redesign at all: it was to build an aggregator-routed mandate fallback for four PSBs and, in the meantime, to bid differently. Sunaina's board line was: "The screen is fine. We changed who is standing in front of it."

Case B — Surangam: the denominator as a commercial instrument

Yusuf's team reconstructed one representative day of 1,000 documents reaching the platform out of 2,300 claims the insurer received.

Every row is an honest funnel. They differ in entry criterion and retry convention alone. The insurer's chief operating officer was measuring the value of a contract against total claims volume, which is the number her own costs scale with; Surangam was measuring the performance of a system against the inputs it was given. The resolution Yusuf proposed was not to win the argument but to restructure it: report all four, define the contractual metric as accepted-per-document-uploaded on a first-attempt basis, and add a jointly-owned intake-coverage metric — documents uploaded over claims received, then 43.5% — with a shared target. The renewal was negotiated on two numbers instead of one, and the intake metric became the largest source of the following year's value.

Case C — Phadwara Learning: where the approach failed

Phadwara Learning, a consumer edtech with three products, imposed a single governed funnel across all of them in 2024: signup, first lesson started, first lesson completed, seven-day streak, paid conversion, with a common seven-day window. The intent was sound — comparability, one definition, no arguing. The failure was that the products had different natural clocks. The 80th-percentile time to complete a first unit was 1.4 days for spoken English, 3.1 days for test-prep and 16.2 days for the coding-for-children product, whose first unit was a multi-session project. The seven-day window truncated most of the coding cohort mid-journey. The governed funnel reported coding activation at 21%; measured at 21 days it was 46%.

Leadership, comparing 21% against 58% and 49%, reallocated ₹1.4 crore of the next year's budget away from coding and lost two engineers to the reorganisation before an analyst reran the cohort with a longer window. The failure was not the governance; it was the assumption that a definition can be shared across products whose completion-time distributions differ by an order of magnitude. The recovery took five months and looked like this: the shared event taxonomy was kept and strengthened, because that was genuinely valuable; the shared funnel definition was abandoned in favour of per-product windows set at each product's observed 80th-percentile completion time and reviewed quarterly; every published funnel acquired a four-line definition header; and cross-product comparisons were made only on window-normalised rates with the windows printed beside them. Coding activation re-measured at 46%, the budget was partially restored two quarters late, and the phrase "same metric, same window" entered the company's vocabulary as a caution rather than an aspiration.

The dilution effect, quantified

One further piece of Praanali arithmetic underwrites the fourth distinction in section 6. In June, Praanali removed two fields from the application form and lifted install-to-application from 41.0% to 46.0%. On 405,000 installs that is 186,300 applications against 166,050 at the old rate — 20,250 marginal applicants. The remaining five steps had historically converted applications to disbursals at 15.78%, so the naive projection was 29,398 loans, a 12.2% lift. The marginal cohort actually converted at 6.7% downstream — their KYC completion was 51% against 70%, and underwriting approved 31% of them against 51% — producing 1,357 loans against the inframarginal 26,203, for 27,560 in total: a 5.2% lift, not 12.2%. Blended application-to-disbursal fell from 15.78% to 14.79%. Three downstream teams opened July having "regressed" because a fourth team had succeeded.

9. Failure Modes and Their Early Warnings

Silent instrumentation drift. Early sign: a step falls sharply on a release date and only on one platform. Diagnostic question: what is this event's fire rate per active session by app version? Cost of late catching: an entire redesign shipped against a tracking bug — at Praanali's scale, roughly six engineer-weeks and a quarter of misdirected roadmap.

The convenient window. Early sign: the window is lengthened in the same meeting where the target is missed. Diagnostic question: what is the 95th-percentile completion time, and when was the window last changed and by whom? Cost late: every historical comparison in the company becomes invalid and nobody knows which quarter the break occurred in.

Step rates as team OKRs. Early sign: two adjacent steps improve while the total does not move. Diagnostic question: has any team changed the entry criterion into its own step this quarter? Cost late: a year of genuine-looking wins with zero business effect, and a metrics function whose credibility has to be rebuilt from scratch.

Ungoverned definitions. Early sign: two analysts answer the same question with numbers that differ by more than five points. Diagnostic question: can you show me the entry criterion, window, order rule and counting unit for both? Cost late: leadership stops trusting funnels and reverts to anecdote, which is far harder to reverse than a wrong number.

Acting on unmatured cohorts. Early sign: recent weeks always look worse and are always revised upward. Diagnostic question: what share of this cohort is still in flight? Cost late: an emergency response to a decline that was never there, and, worse, a subsequent recovery that gets credited to the response.

Mistaking the funnel for the roadmap. Early sign: three consecutive quarters of step-level optimisation with a flat total. Diagnostic question: what would the funnel look like if this step did not exist? Cost late: a competitor removes the step entirely — Praanali's pre-approved offer flow for existing bank customers skips KYC and underwriting for a third of applicants — and incremental optimisation cannot catch a structural change.

10. Where Experts Genuinely Disagree

Should gates sit inside the funnel? The inclusion camp argues that the business cares about installs-to-disbursals and that hiding underwriting declines lets product congratulate itself on a rate that never reaches the bank account; the funnel should model reality, and reality includes rejection. The exclusion camp argues that a funnel is an instrument for directing product work and that any step product cannot move is noise that dominates the decomposition — at Praanali the gate is the single largest loss in the chain and would anchor every conversation. For the inclusion camp to be wrong, it would have to be shown that teams reliably ignore a clearly-labelled gate; for the exclusion camp to be wrong, it would have to be shown that separating the funnels causes leadership to lose sight of the end-to-end economics. Both failures are observed in practice, which is why the disagreement persists.

One governed funnel, or many question-specific ones? The governance camp rests on the evidence of organisations paralysed by duelling numbers, and on the fact that comparability over time is itself a product feature of a metric. The flexibility camp rests on Phadwara: a governed definition applied across heterogeneous products produced a confidently wrong answer that cost ₹1.4 crore, and the governance apparatus made it harder, not easier, to question. The governance camp would be wrong if definitional discipline could be had at the level of events rather than funnels; the flexibility camp would be wrong if ad-hoc funnels in practice converge rather than diverge. Phadwara's recovery is evidence for a middle position that neither camp fully holds.

Are funnel-derived uplift projections worth making? The causal camp's position is that the dilution arithmetic in section 8 is general, not a Praanali peculiarity: any upstream improvement admits a lower-intent margin, so projections are systematically optimistic and should be replaced by experiments. The planning camp's rejoinder is that an upper bound is still decision-relevant — if the best case is 1,065 loans a month and the work costs six weeks, you can decline it without running anything — and that an organisation which refuses to estimate before testing simply tests in a worse order. The causal camp would be wrong if the marginal population converted at rates close to the inframarginal; that is an empirical question, and at Praanali the answer was 6.7% against 15.78%.

Linear funnel or path graph? The journey camp holds that for products with many entry points and heavy re-entry — most modern consumer apps, most AI tools — a linear funnel is a fiction maintained for the comfort of slide decks, and that state-transition analysis is the honest representation. The funnel camp's steelman is not that journeys are linear but that decisions are: a team must choose one thing to fix, and a Sankey diagram with forty transitions does not produce a choice, whereas a deliberately lossy projection does. The strongest version of this position concedes the fiction and defends it as a decision-forcing device.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has merely studied funnels builds one correctly. Someone who has internalised them behaves differently in four visible ways. They state the four definitional choices before the numbers, so that disagreement is forced upward into the definition rather than left to fester under the chart. They never present a step-to-step table without at least one segmentation beside it, because they expect mix shift rather than merely tolerating the possibility. They distinguish, out loud and by name, between the step that lost the most and the step worth the most, and they carry a rough reachable-headroom estimate for each candidate rather than a wish. And they treat every projected uplift as an upper bound, saying so unprompted, which is how Sunaina kept a board from budgeting 2,486 loans a month against work that could deliver 1,065.

There is a fifth, subtler sign. Experts know when to stop building funnels. When the honest answer to "what would this look like if the step did not exist" is interesting, they put the instrument down and design instead. The funnel is a tool for improving a path; it is silent, by construction, on whether the path deserves to exist.

12. The Decisions

Sunaina went to the 26 September board with a two-part recommendation and an explicit hierarchy. First, a one-week reversal of the video-KYC liveness threshold, sized at 1,164 loans a month with high confidence because the change was self-inflicted and dated. Second, a six-week PSB mandate fallback built through a payment aggregator, sized at 1,065 loans a month with the reachable-headroom caveat stated on the slide. Third, and the part she considered most important, a change to how acquisition was bought: the August tier-2 push had shifted the bank mix by 35 points and should be bid to a cost-per-disbursal target by bank cohort rather than a cost-per-install target. She declined to propose any work on the underwriting gate and said why. Her stated reasoning was that the funnel had told her where to look, segmentation had told her what had actually changed, and only the reachable-headroom estimate had told her what to do — and that the three are routinely confused.

Yusuf chose not to resolve the 60.9%-versus-26.0% dispute in Surangam's favour. He proposed a contract amendment defining the renewal metric as first-attempt accepted-per-document-uploaded, published all four rates monthly, and added a jointly-owned intake-coverage target. He accepted a metric that read 54.1% against a 55% threshold — a number Surangam missed in month one — because he judged that a metric the customer believed was worth more than a metric Surangam could defend. The intake work that followed raised coverage from 43.5% to 61% over two quarters, which moved more value than any model improvement that year.

Discussion questions. (1) Praanali's underwriting gate was excluded from the product funnel on the grounds that product cannot move it. Under what circumstances does that exclusion become self-serving, and what would you require to be published alongside the product funnel to prevent it? (2) Surangam adopted the definition that was worse for Surangam. Was that a defensible commercial judgement or an avoidable concession, and what evidence would settle it? (3) Phadwara's governed funnel was both the cause of a ₹1.4 crore error and, in its recovered form, the thing that prevented the next one. What exactly should be governed centrally, and what should be delegated to product teams?

13. Going Deeper

  • Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — the ordered ARM actions are the raw material of every funnel; choosing them badly is the error you cannot fix downstream.
  • Designing an event taxonomy — the funnels you can build in 2027 are decided by the events you name today; this is the highest-leverage upstream skill.
  • Reading drop-off — the interpretive craft that begins where the table ends: turning a step loss into a hypothesis worth testing.
  • Defining activation (the aha moment) — picks which step in the funnel is the one that predicts retention, converting a flow metric into a leading indicator.
  • Feature adoption analysis — applies funnel logic to a single feature's exposure-to-habit path, where entry criteria are subtler than in a purchase flow.
  • Estimating feature impact — supplies the reachable-headroom discipline that turns the leverage table in section 3 from arithmetic into a plan.
  • Attribution and its limits — explains why the top of the funnel resists causal assignment, and why cost-per-install misleads when the bank mix moves.
  • Device telemetry and fleet analytics — the reconciliation practice Doabgrid needed: what a funnel looks like when the first three steps are physical.
  • Metrics by funnel stage — which metric belongs at which step, so that step owners are not all optimising the same number.
  • Landing pages and conversion copy — the craft layer at the widest step, where small copy changes produce the marginal, lower-intent population section 8 warns about.
  • E-commerce and quick-commerce product management — the domain where funnel practice is most mature and where basket and slot mechanics complicate the ordering rule.
  • Cohort analysis — the technique that makes maturity windows and censoring tractable rather than a source of false alarms.
  • Retention curves and the PMF signal — the orthogonal measurement: whether the users your funnel converted were worth converting.
  • Stickiness and natural frequency — sets how often a user re-enters the funnel, which determines whether a window of a day or a month is honest.
  • Segmenting users in analytics — the direct antidote to the mix-shift failure that dominated Praanali's August.
  • Root cause analysis of a metric change — the method that takes over once the funnel has narrowed the search to one step.
  • Signal vs noise; product vs measurement — how to tell a real step decline from sampling variation or an SDK upgrade, which is the first check, not the last.
